newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African shares seen hugging levels next week.
newsitem.headline: S.African shares seen hugging levels next week.

text.p: A dearth of company earnings and economic reports, coupled with fresh jitters about U.S. markets after two losing days, is seen strapping South African shares into a tight range next week, analysts said Friday.
They said stocks' recent flat performance, when the Johannesburg market's overall index was trapped in a narrow 30-point band for most of this week, was likely to be repeated.
"I think it will continue to drift around, it might come up a bit, but more likely it will be slightly softer," said Willi Jonker, executive director of portfolio management at Norwich Investments.

Fund managers and dealers said the market had recently been overshadowed by a lack of interest from local institutions and foreign participants, who were seen able, but unlikely, to release stocks from their torpid state.
"Our most important question is what (foreign investors) appetite is? We just get the feeling that their minds are elsewhere," Jonker told Reuters.
The recent lacklustre market was also blamed on the wider investment avenues available to South Africans as exchange control regulations are eased.
Old Mutual, South Africa's biggest investment group, said this week it was concluding a new asset swap programme to increase its offshore holdings.
Selwyn Feldman, managing director of Old Mutual Unit Trusts, said that the firm had approval to accumulate a total of 970 million rand in foreign assets.
The March budget gave institutions the go ahead to invest up to 10 percent of their total assets abroad and not, as before, 10 percent of each individual mutual fund, known locally as unit trusts.
From July 1, private individuals will also be able to invest abroad an as yet unstipulated amount.

Although asset swaps imply an opposite investment in South Africa by foreign players there have been concerns that the mechanism is failing to secure offshore monies, resulting in a net outflow of funds and no increased demand for shares.
Dealers on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange said they expected more asset swaps, a few of which have taken place this week, to continue to pass through the market.
"Volumes have been dismal except for asset swaps and some futures basket trading. That's what's been keeping (daily) turnover quite high," one trader said.

As no major South African companies are due to report results next week, eyes will be focused on the start of the gold quarterly reporting season. Results kick off next Thursday with Gold Fields of South Africa Ltd.
But the outlook for gold shares next week remained bleak.
"Technically (bullion) looks very weak. It keeps making lower lows and lower highs. Shares will continue to drift," said another portfolio manager who asked not to be identified.
